entries.title: open the README with what the name stands for, and mark stage0's src/ citations
entries.body:
The README now leads with the repository description: Native Instruction
Static Host AKA Turbo Typescript, a fast subset of TypeScript without the
encumbrance of JavaScript.

Comments and documents cite the deleted stage0 compiler by its old paths
(`src/checker/arrays.ts`, `src/types.ts`, ...). Every such citation now
reads "stage0's `src/...`", so it cannot be mistaken for a pointer into the
tree: nine of those names match a module of the current compiler. The
fixture sources in `tests/cases/`, the goldens and the changelog are left
as written.

entries.title: rename every tracked path to kebab-case
entries.body:
Step 1 of the cleanup pass in `.claude/linting.md`: renames only. The
22 snake_case modules of `self/` (`emit_arrays.ts` is `emit-arrays.ts`),
the cookbook snippets and their `.args`, the benchmarks, the test
harness scripts and fixtures under `tests/self/`, `tests/ir/` and
`tests/layout/`, and the three runtime halves are kebab-case, and every
import, script, workflow and document that names them follows. The
fixture trees (`tests/cases`, `tests/link`, `tests/wordings`,
`tests/differential/corpus`) keep their names, as the rule says.

What moves with the names and nothing else: `tests/self/goldens/` and
`docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md` are regenerated, and differ from before only in
the spelling of the paths and the order the new names sort in. A
cookbook listing or a benchmark is still called by its file name, so
`bench/run.mjs` and `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` spell them with hyphens now.
`scripts/check-filenames.mjs` exempts a `node_modules` directory,
because that is the name package resolution looks for, and with that it
prints nothing.

Measured: 179 paths renamed; `check-filenames.mjs` 179 -> 0; Biome 1366 -> 1214 warnings
Refs: .claude/linting.md

BREAKING CHANGE: the runtime sources the npm package ships are now
`runtime/runtime-os.c`, `runtime/runtime-parallel.c` and
`runtime/runtime-wasm.c` (were `runtime_os.c`, `runtime_parallel.c` and
`runtime_wasm.c`). `--link` finds them itself; a build that compiles
them by hand has to follow the new names.

entries.title: apply Biome's autofixes
entries.body:
Step 2 of the cleanup pass in `.claude/linting.md`: `biome lint --write`,
then the unsafe fix for `useBlockStatements` alone, read before it was
committed. Every `if`, `else` and loop body has braces now. A template
with no `${}` is a plain string, a Yoda comparison reads the other way
round, and one `let` that is never reassigned is a `const`. Nothing is
reformatted beyond what a fix needed.

The compiler's IR does not move. `self/` compiled by the same compiler
before and after the fixes gives byte-identical `.ll` for every module
of `compile.ts` and of the three dump entry points. The `tests/self`
checked-dump goldens are regenerated, and differ only in the columns a
new brace moved and in that one `const`.
metrics: Biome 1214 -> 256 warnings; self/ IR byte-identical (69 modules)

entries.title: clear the lint backlog by hand, and make every function an arrow
entries.body:
Step 3 of the cleanup pass in `.claude/linting.md`. `npm run lint` now
reports no warnings.

- **Every `function` declaration is an arrow bound to a `const`**: 142
  in the JavaScript tooling and 75 in the Nish programs (`std/`,
  `examples/`, `docs/cookbook/`, `bench/`, `tests/self/`), which join
  the compiler under the `no-function-declaration` plugin.
  `docs/cookbook/fn-add-function.ts` keeps its `function`, because that
  listing exists to show the spelling. A `const` is not hoisted, so every
  converted file was checked for module-level code that reaches a
  function before its definition.
- **No shadowed names**: 45 locals and parameters that hid an outer
  binding are renamed, with the language service rather than by text.
- **Unused imports** are gone, and no test module re-exports what it
  imports.
- **Nested ternaries** are `if`/`else` chains, and each empty block says
  why it is empty.
- `useParseIntRadix` is off for Nish programs, because the builtin
  `parseInt` takes one argument, and `useForOf` is off everywhere,
  because six of its seven hits were argument parsers that consume a
  value with `argv[++i]`.

entries.title: format the tree with Biome, without semicolons
entries.body:
Step 4 of the cleanup pass in `.claude/linting.md`, together with its
step 7. The formatter now writes semicolons only where JavaScript's
insertion rule needs one (`"semicolons": "asNeeded"`), and
`npm run format` has run over everything Biome reads. The fixtures in
`tests/cases/` keep theirs, because the formatter does not read them.
Semicolon-free sources need a compiler that accepts them; 0.12.0 is the
first release that does, and it is the seed the compiler is built with.

The compiler's IR does not move: every module's `.ll` is byte-identical
before and after the pass. What does move is text other files quote or
scrape. The `tests/self` goldens, `docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md` and three `-g`
goldens that step into `std/` are regenerated, differing only in line
and column numbers. The registry checker, the `tests/run.js` checks
that read the compiler's sources, and the version bump in
`release-pr.yml` match with or without a semicolon.

entries.title: make every lint rule an error, and add the checks a clean tree allows
entries.body:
Steps 5, 6, 8 and 10 of the cleanup pass, which ends here.
`.claude/linting.md` now describes the gates rather than a backlog.

- **Every Biome rule is an `error`**, the `no-function-declaration`
  plugin included, and `npm run lint` is `biome check .` with the
  formatter on, so formatting is a gate. The file-name check runs

- **knip** (`npm run lint:dead` and a CI step) finds no unused file,

  other module imports are internal now, and six were dead code.
- **shellcheck** runs in CI at `-S warning`, with its eight findings

- **A `PostToolUse` hook** formats each file an agent edits, and
  `npm run lint:fix` does the same for a person.
- **`.git-blame-ignore-revs`** lists the two style-only commits.
- `organizeImports` stays off: sorting reorders declarations in the IR
  of 36 of the compiler's 69 modules.

entries.title: parallelReduce under Node, and NL2348 at the call for a non-scalar reduce
entries.body:
`parallelReduce` now prints the same natively and under Node's documented prelude path, and a reduce over `string` or class elements is refused with one NL2348 at the user's call, naming the type.

**Under Node (#224).** `reduceBlockCount` and `reduceBlockStart` in `std/threads.ts` computed in `i64`. Under the prelude, `toI64` is a BigInt, and a BigInt throws when it meets a number, so every reduce threw. Both functions now compute in `f64`. Every value they reach is exact there (`n * k < 2^37`), so the blocks, and with them wp29 §11's determinism contract, are unchanged. A cross-check of 14.7M `(n, k)` pairs against the BigInt definition found no mismatch. Both functions also lose their divide-by-zero path and become `nounwind willreturn readnone`. `nish/threads` already resolved under the prelude's resolve hook, and `docs/RUN_UNDER_NODE.md` now says so.

**At the call (#225).** A reduce's `T` is its element, its identity and its result. Instantiating the std body for a `string` or a class used to report five errors inside `std/threads.ts`. `reduceElementMessage` in `src/parallel.ts` now answers before instantiation, from `checkGenericCall`. It reuses the map rule's wording, so the program gets one NL2348 at its own call.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#data-parallelism-nishthreads, docs/wp29-thread-surface.md
Tests: tests/link/par_reduce_blocks, tests/cases/reject_par_reduce_result_type, tests/cases/reject_par_reduce_result_class, and a tests/run.js check that runs par_map and par_reduce under Node against the native output

Fixes #224
Fixes #225

entries.title: a surrogate-pair escape is the code point it spells
entries.body:
A high-surrogate escape (`\uD800`–`\uDBFF`) written immediately before a low-surrogate escape (`\uDC00`–`\uDFFF`) now encodes as the four UTF-8 bytes of the one code point it spells. Before, the lexer encoded each half separately, as six bytes of CESU-8. So the pair escape of U+1F600 was not `===` to the emoji, its `length` was 6, a `Map` key set with one spelling was not found with the other, and printing it wrote invalid UTF-8. Either half may be written `\uXXXX` or `\u{…}`, in plain and template literals alike.

**A lone surrogate** still encodes on its own as three bytes (WTF-8), as before. `docs/LANGUAGE.md` now states that rule. Pairs are joined only inside one literal: concatenating two halves at run time gives six bytes, which is a stated divergence from JavaScript.

**A braced escape above `0x10FFFF` is refused**, in TypeScript's words: "An extended Unicode escape value must be between 0x0 and 0x10FFFF inclusive". It used to accumulate in `i32` without a bound, so `\u{10000D800}` wrapped into the surrogate range.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md (String literals)
Tests: tests/cases/str_surrogate_pair, tests/cases/str_surrogate_map_key, tests/cases/str_surrogate_lone, tests/cases/reject_surrogate_escape_too_large, tests/cases/reject_surrogate_escape_wraps

Fixes #246
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: a stored Result is not a discard, and Map of Result compiles
entries.body:
`new Map<string, Result<i32, string>>()` could not be compiled at all. The must-handle rule (NL2025) fired inside `std/collections.ts`, on `items[to] = items[from]` and on `items.pop()`. The fix changes three things about how a `Result` is handed on.

**An assignment moves a `Result`; it does not drop one.** `rs[0] = rs[1]` and `r2 = r1` now compile. `r2 = r1` reads `r1`, and `r2`, a local, must still be inspected. The value an assignment replaces is dropped, though, so a new rule, **NL2377**, refuses assigning a `Result` local again while the value it holds has not been read since it was written. That closes the hole the exemption would otherwise open (`let r = f(); r = g();` losing `f()`'s failure).

The check reads the function in source order, right-hand side before target. It is not a control-flow graph: a read in either branch of an `if` counts. An element or a field is not tracked slot by slot. `docs/LANGUAGE.md` states all of this.

**A discard in a generic body is judged against the template's declared type**, as Rust's `#[must_use]` is. `items.pop()` on `items: T[]` drops a `T`, which is no longer refused at `T = Result`. A template that drops a `Result<T, E>` it declared is still refused at every instantiation. When the origin cannot be followed, the judgement fails closed.

**Two emitter bugs hidden behind the compile error are fixed.**
- A missed `get` on such a map now answers `null` where it answered `0` into a pointer.
- A packable `Result<i32, i32>` Map value is now packed and unpacked across `valueAt`, `setValueAt` and `insertAt`. Without that, it linked and then segfaulted.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md (Result, rule 1)
Tests: tests/cases/map_value_result, tests/cases/map_value_result_by_value, tests/cases/res_result_store, tests/cases/res_result_store_flow, tests/cases/reject_result_store_unread, tests/cases/reject_result_overwrite_unread, tests/cases/reject_result_store_loop_unread, tests/cases/reject_result_generic_discarded

Fixes #233

entries.title: a proof never leaves a proof consumer, and an assignment ends a narrowing in an && chain
entries.body:
Two soundness holes in narrowing are closed. Both let a program `tsc` refuses compile, and then read garbage natively where Node throws.

**A `Result`'s proof no longer leaks (#234).** An identifier narrowed to `ok` used to carry that proof into anything its value flowed into: a ternary arm, an array literal, an unannotated `let`. So `const z = r.value > 0 ? r : q` with `q` an `Err` typed `z` as proven, and `z.value` compiled and read the error's payload as a value. Now a proof is visible only to a proof consumer: the receiver of `.ok`, `.value`, `.error`, `isOk()`, `isErr()`, `unwrapOr`, `expect` or `orReturn`, or a narrowing test. Anywhere else, the value is the unproven `Result`. `const y = r` inside a narrowing therefore loses the proof. That refuses a few programs `tsc` accepts, which is the safe direction, and `docs/LANGUAGE.md` says so. `T | null` narrowing never leaked this way, because a narrowed nullable is a different type.

**An assignment inside an `&&`/`||` chain ends a narrowing (#235).** In `p !== null && g((p = null) === null) && p.v > 0`, the checker re-applied `p`'s narrowing after the middle operand set `p` to `null`. Now an operand that assigns a narrowed variable ends its narrowing for every later operand, for `T | null` and `Result` alike. This is the rule `assignInto` already applies between statements.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md (narrowing, Result)
Tests: tests/cases/reject_result_ternary_keeps_proof, reject_result_array_keeps_proof, reject_result_let_keeps_proof, reject_null_narrowing_assigned_in_chain, reject_result_narrowing_assigned_in_chain, res_proof_consumers

Fixes #234

entries.title: a misplaced numeric separator is refused in TypeScript's words
entries.body:
A numeric separator that is not between two digits is now refused by the lexer with TypeScript's own wording, as one `NL0001` syntax error per literal:

- "Numeric separators are not allowed here" (TS6188). Examples: `0x_FF`, `10_`, `0xFF_n`, `1_.5`, `1e_5`, `1e5_` and `0_1`.
- "Multiple consecutive numeric separators are not permitted" (TS6189). Examples: `1__0` and `0xF__F`.

Before this, a later phase refused the literal and named a rule it had not broken. `0x_FF` was reported as not fitting in i32, for example.

Separators in the right place now work as well. The parser removes them from a number's text, so `1_000_000`, `0xFF_FF`, `9_007_199_254_740_991`, `1_234.5_6` and `1e1_0` compile at their values, where before the first two were refused.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#numeric-literals
Tests: tests/cases/math_numeric_separators, tests/cases/reject_separator_*
Fixes #263

entries.title: a parameter or local named like an emitter label compiles
entries.body:
LLVM keeps a function's arguments, blocks and allocas in one namespace, and the emitter wrote each parameter as `%<name>`, as the source spelled it. Two names the emitter writes itself have no dot, so a parameter could collide with them:

- `entry`, the block every function opens with. `const f = (entry: i32): i32 => entry + 1` produced IR that `llvm-as` refused (`unable to create block named 'entry'`).
- `chr`, the one-byte slot `String.fromCharCode` allocates, which a parameter of that name defined twice.

A parameter with either name is now written `%entry.param` or `%chr.param`. That happens in the `define`, at every read, in the packed-`Result` prologue, and in the `-g` `llvm.dbg.value` line. The debug record keeps the source name.

Locals were never affected, because a local's slot is `%<name>.addr`. The IR of every other program is byte-identical.

Tests: tests/cases/reserved_label_names, tests/cases/reserved_label_names_dbg
Fixes #266
Part of #257
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: threads P2, using s = scope() and s.spawn(fn, arg)
entries.body:
A scope runs unlike tasks on threads of their own, and every task is joined before its block is left:

```ts
import { scope } from "nish/threads";
{
  using s = scope();
  s.spawn(sumOf, xs, sums, 0);           // sums[0] = sumOf(xs)
  s.spawn(primesBelow, 1000, counts, 0); // counts[0] = primesBelow(1000)
}                                        // joined here, on every exit
```

`using` is read as a contextual keyword, a flag on the existing variable declaration, and it binds only `scope()`. A scope is only ever the receiver of a `spawn`, so it cannot leave its block.

The join is emitted at every exit of the block: its end, a `return` (before the returned value is computed), and a `break` or `continue` that leaves it. It always comes before any arena release.

A task runs, and its answer is stored with `dst[at] = entry(arg)`, when the scope joins. The first task runs on the calling thread and each other on a thread of its own. Every answer is then stored on the calling thread in spawn order, so two tasks naming one slot are ordered and never race.

A task is held to the data-parallel rules: it writes nothing its caller can see, controls no arena, and answers a number, a `boolean` or an enum. Its entry is a named top-level function.

Under Node, `spawn` runs the task and stores its answer at once. NL2394 keeps the two meanings the same:
- a destination is a `const` local bound to a fresh array that is never handed on;
- between a scope's first spawn and its block's end, the program may not read a destination or write memory a task could read.

N tasks over N arrays compile, and every program that could tell the two apart is refused. `using` needs `--js-explicit-resource-management` on Node 22 and is native from Node 24.

New codes NL2387–NL2394.

Measured: 3.30x on four unlike tasks on 4 cores (examples/tasks.ts: 1.806 s sequential, 0.547 s as one scope)
Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#scoped-tasks, docs/wp29-thread-surface.md
Tests: tests/link/thread_scope_basic, thread_scope_exit_paths, thread_scope_many_arrays, thread_scope_nested_arena, tests/cases/reject_thread_*
Part of #257
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: a binary, octal, exponent or separated literal reads its true value
entries.body:
Every numeric-literal spelling the language accepts is now read at the value it spells, in every numeric type.

- `1e5` as an `i32` was 245, which was a silent miscompile. The integer reader took the `e` for the hex digit 14. It is now 100000.
- `0b1010` and `0o17` were refused as "does not fit in i32", because the runtime's `Number` reads them as NaN. They are now 10 and 15.
- `1_000` is 1000 in every type.

One reader, `numericLiteralValue`, turns a literal's text into the double TypeScript reads. It drops separators, and it reads `0b`/`0o` through hexadecimal, so a literal past 2^53 rounds once, as TypeScript rounds it. Everything that reads a literal as a number now goes through it:
- the fit and fraction checks;
- the emitter's constants;
- ranged-type bounds;
- module constants, enum members and case labels;
- the loop analyses.

An exponent counts as a fraction only when it leaves one: `1e3` is 1000, `100e-2` is 1, and `1e-1` is refused in integer position. An `i64` module constant past 2^53 (`1e19`) is now refused in the words an `i64` literal already had. Before, it was refused as a non-integer or folded to wrapped bits.

Decimal and hexadecimal programs keep byte-identical IR.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#numeric-literals
Tests: tests/cases/literal_spellings, tests/cases/reject_literal_*
Fixes #267
Part of #257
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: prove range entries and index through declared ranges (WP31)
entries.body:
A declared range is now a fact the bounds proof reads. A range check that the program already makes unnecessary is not emitted, and one left inside a loop warns.

- **The type answers; nothing is stored.** `integer<Lo, Hi>`, and the unsigned widths' own ranges, give an index its non-negativity and its upper bound. A `u8`/`u16`/ranged local is an index type. `const k = toI32(b)` of one records `k < Hi + 1`. Every write into a ranged place is an entry, so there is no fact to forget.
- **Every range entry is judged** at the point where it is checked. A local proven inside the range, by a guard, a loop bound or an earlier check, enters with no check at all. So does `toI32` of a range that fits. The proof is kept per instantiation. The function's attributes lose the panic tail when every entry in it is proven.
- **NL9013**, a performance warning, fires for an unproven entry inside a loop. It names the guard that would prove it, or it suggests binding a computed value to an `i32` local. It is silent outside loops, silent under `--no-warn-performance`, and unaffected by `--unchecked-indexing`.

wp31 §12's `getByte` program, with the index declared `integer<0, 255>`, now compiles `getByte`, `sumCalled` and `sumInline` to `{ nounwind willreturn readonly }` with no bounds or range check left. That is the attribute `sumInline` had before the range.

Refs: docs/wp31-ranged-integers.md §8, docs/LANGUAGE.md
Tests: tests/cases/perf_rng_getbyte, perf_rng_quiet, perf_rng_loop, perf_rng_counter, arr_bounds_ranged
Part of #257

entries.title: a numeric literal with a leading zero is refused in TypeScript's words
entries.body:
A decimal literal that starts with `0` and another digit is now refused by the lexer in TypeScript's words, as one `NL0001` syntax error per literal:

- a run of octal digits (`017`, `00`, `07n`) gets TS1121, `Octal literals are not allowed. Use the syntax '0o17'`, naming the `0o` spelling of the same digits;
- any other run (`09`, `08.5`) gets TS1489, `Decimals with leading zeros are not allowed`.

Before, `const x: i32 = 017` compiled and printed 17, a value neither `tsc` nor Node gives it, since both refuse the file.

`0`, `0.5`, `0e1`, `0x…`, `0b…` and `0o…` stay legal. So does a zero inside a fraction or an exponent (`1.05`, `1e05`). The leading-zero error outranks a separator later in the literal, as it does in `tsc`.

Refs: docs/LANGUAGE.md#numeric-literals
Tests: tests/cases/reject_leading_zero_octal, tests/cases/reject_leading_zero_decimal, tests/cases/leading_zero_legal
Fixes #271

entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: ranged parameters at the host boundary (WP31)
entries.body:
An exported function with an `integer<Lo, Hi>` parameter is now safe to call from a C, N-API or wasm host.

- **Where the check lives follows the linkage.** A function that `--strict-exports` makes `internal` keeps each check at its call sites, where the facts are. Any other function checks its ranged parameters in its own prologue, because a host may pass any `int32_t`. Its Nish callers then skip their own check. A C host that passes a value out of range gets the panic it would get anywhere else.
- **The bridges throw first.** The N-API shim reads the argument as a double. The wasm loader judges the number itself before the engine's ToInt32 could wrap it. Outside the range, both throw `RangeError: pick: argument 2 (day) must be an integer in [1, 7]`, 4294967301 included. A value that is not a number throws `TypeError`. `--emit-napi-async` rejects with the same error.
- **The sidecars say so.** The C header spells the parameter `int32_t`, with its range and what leaving it does above the prototype; it compiles under `-std=c11 -Wall -Wextra -Werror -pedantic`. The `.d.ts` spells it `number` and names the `RangeError`. A range inside data (an array, a record, a `Result`) is not described.

NL9013 no longer warns about an argument its callee checks in its own prologue.

Refs: docs/wp31-ranged-integers.md §9, docs/LANGUAGE.md (Interop)
Tests: tests/cases/interop_rng_param, interop_rng_host (+ .c host), interop_rng_loop; tests/run.js "interop_rng"

entries.title: plan the round trip between TypeScript and Nish, at zero native cost (WP33)
entries.body:
A new work package, WP33, plans how a program moves in both directions
between TypeScript and Nish. On the way in, an agent ports a TypeScript
project by driving the compiler. On the way out, `--emit ts` turns a Nish
program into TypeScript that runs on Node, Bun or a browser and means
what the native build meant. Nothing is built yet.

The deciding constraint is that neither direction may cost the native
build anything. Every stage is a compile-time analysis, a diagnostic, or
TypeScript the compiler writes out, and none changes a lowering. So no
`.ll` golden moves, and `bench/instructions.json` is never raised for it.
Where JavaScript's meaning is the slower one, Nish's meaning stays: it
becomes a translation on the way out and a flagged site on the way in.

The note sorts every difference between a program's two readings into
four classes: identical; a safety net, where native stops and TypeScript
carries on with a wrong value; translated; and untranslatable, which the
language may never add. It keeps a ledger of every known difference, and
it records six decisions, each chosen to keep native speed:

- strings stay UTF-8 bytes;
- `slice` keeps its check, since JavaScript's clamp costs 13 instructions
  a call and can never be proven away;
- arrays of records stay contiguous, with the aliasing flagged on the way
  in;
- the typed-array names lose `push` and `pop`;
- `--json` gains a `fix` field;
- `number` stays i32 in strict mode and f64 in compat mode.

RUN_UNDER_NODE.md gains four divergences it did not list: `slice` bounds,
record copies into arrays, `new Array<T>(n)` holes, and `push` on the
typed-array names. The construct checklist in ARCHITECTURE.md now asks
every construct for its TypeScript reading.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: plan hosting cs, starting with its relay on a network stack in std
entries.body:
* docs(wp33): plan what the compiler owes the port of cs

A second corpus beside the compiler itself: a browser arena shooter and
its servers, which the owner wants written entirely in Nish. The note
measures first. The released 0.12.0 parsed none of the game's source
files, and every first refusal was something the game rewrites on its
own side, such as an inline `type` import, `as const`, a regex or `?.`.
So the list is drawn from what the game *does*, and each item names
the part of it that cannot be written without it.

There are fourteen items: exported enums and aliases, JavaScript's zero
and the missing `Math`, a wall clock and entropy, and an `--overlap`
flag that refuses anything meaning two things under V8 and natively.
The flag carries most weight, since the port rewrites in place and runs
one source in both meanings for months. Then come `std/crypto`, typed
JSON, host imports on `wasm`, programs that do not exit, sockets and a
loop the program owns (wp24's refusal of `async` stands), HTTP and
WebSocket, processes, WP27's remaining stages, and discriminated
unions. The game's repository holds the port's own order and its
cutover gates in `docs/nish-port.md`.

Refs: docs/wp33-hosting-cs.md

* docs(wp34): start the cs port with its relay, on a Nish network stack

The owner set the order: the port of cs begins with the Rust half of
its game server. That is the relay, which terminates WebTransport and
forwards game datagrams over UDP. It is rebuilt in Nish on a network
stack that serves HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 with streaming bodies,
raw sockets and WebTransport. The note moves from WP33 to WP34, because
WP33 is now the round trip between TypeScript and Nish. Its separate
overlap flag is withdrawn in favour of WP33's portability class.

The relay goes first because it computes nothing the game does. Its
contracts are two byte formats already pinned by fixtures, so it
carries none of the port's determinism risk. It is also the edge a
native game server needs before it can take a player.

Phase one asks the compiler and runtime for five things: exported
enums, byte plumbing, a clock and entropy, sockets with an epoll loop
the program owns (wp24's refusal of `async` stands), and constant-time
builtins. Memory stays bounded without a new model, because pools are
sized from the relay's caps. The stack is seventeen lanes in a package
of its own, and most of them are proved by their RFC's own test vectors
before a socket exists. The TLS 1.3 handshake is one state machine,
carried by TLS records over TCP and by CRYPTO frames over QUIC.

Refs: docs/wp34-hosting-cs.md

* docs(wp34): put the network stack in the standard library

The owner decided where the stack lives: in `std/`, not in a package
of its own. This follows wp26's line. A builtin exists for a syscall,
and everything the language can express is a module. So the sockets
and the loop become a builtin module, `nish:net`, beside `nish:fs`
and `nish:io`. Everything above them becomes `nish/crypto/*` and
`nish/net/*`, and multi-segment `nish/` specifiers already resolve.

What it buys is what wp26 §1a measured: a std module compiles into its
importer, so the attribute fixpoint sees through it and dead code is
stripped. What it costs is cadence, since cs can use a stack lane only
once a release carries it. The interop suites run as a CI job of their
own, beside `npm test`. The note also corrects S5 to match its own wave
table: the stack serves the game's HTTP once the relay is live.

Refs: docs/wp34-hosting-cs.md
